events.n: Accounting tablets from Uruk count in units of 60; the later Babylonian place-value form survives in our 60-minute hours and 360-degree circles.

events.t: Step Pyramid of Djoser, the first monumental stone building
events.n: Credited to the official Imhotep, six stacked stone terraces mark the start of large-scale cut-stone architecture.
Squared to the cardinal points with remarkable accuracy, it stayed the tallest human-made structure for close to four thousand years.
An Old Babylonian clay tablet lists whole-number sides of right triangles more than a thousand years before Pythagoras.

events.t: Babylonians record the cycle of Venus
events.n: Twenty-one years of Venus appearing and vanishing, observed under King Ammisaduqa, among the oldest astronomical records kept.

events.t: Edwin Smith Papyrus, the oldest surgical treatise
events.n: Forty-eight injury cases, each with examination, diagnosis and treatment, including the earliest known written account of the brain.

events.t: Ebers Papyrus records hundreds of remedies
events.n: A long Egyptian medical scroll on the heart, eyes, skin and digestion, with some 700 prescriptions and spells.
The scribe Ahmes copies 84 problems on fractions, areas, volumes and equations, with a value for π close to 3.16.
The oldest surviving water clock, an alabaster vessel from the reign of Amenhotep III, tells the night hours by its outflow.
Divination bones from the Shang capital note eclipses of the Moon, the earliest Chinese astronomical records.
Night-by-night records of the Moon, planets, weather and prices, kept for some six centuries: antiquity’s longest scientific record.

events.t: Sushruta Samhita: surgery in ancient India
events.n: A Sanskrit treatise describing hundreds of operations and instruments, including rebuilding the nose with a flap of skin.
Herodotus reports that Thales foretold the eclipse that stopped a battle between the Lydians and the Medes.

events.t: Tunnel of Eupalinos dug from both ends
events.n: A kilometre-long aqueduct tunnel cut from two sides that met near the middle, an early triumph of applied geometry.
The community Pythagoras led at Croton treats number as the key to the world; the right-triangle theorem carries his name.

events.t: Alcmaeon places the mind in the brain
events.n: From dissection he traces the optic nerves and argues that the brain, not the heart, is the seat of perception and thought.
Everything is made of tiny indivisible particles moving in empty space, a guess chemistry would vindicate two millennia later.

events.t: Hippocratic medicine: disease has natural causes
events.n: The Hippocratic writings explain illness without the gods and stress observation, prognosis and a physician’s duties.

events.t: Eudoxus: proportion, exhaustion and nested spheres
events.n: A theory of ratios that copes with irrational lengths, the method of exhaustion, and the first geometric model of the planets.

events.t: Aristotle’s History of Animals founds zoology
events.n: Hundreds of species, many studied on Lesbos, described and grouped by anatomy, reproduction and way of life.
Thirteen books that derive geometry and number theory from definitions and axioms, the model of proof for two thousand years.
Some 500 plants described by form, habitat and use, earning Aristotle’s successor the title of father of botany.
Systematic human dissection separates nerves from tendons, describes the brain’s ventricles and ties the pulse to the heart.

events.t: Aristarchus puts the Sun at the centre
events.n: Reckoning that the Sun is far larger than the Earth, he proposes that the Earth goes round it, 1,800 years before Copernicus.
A floating body displaces its own weight of fluid; with the law of the lever, the first results of statics and hydrostatics.
Polygons of 96 sides drawn inside and outside a circle squeeze π between two fractions, an early limit argument.

events.t: Ctesibius: the force pump and a self-regulating clock
events.n: Machines driven by air and water pressure, including a float-regulated water clock that set the pattern for centuries.
Noon shadows at Syene and Alexandria give a circumference close to the true 40,000 km.
Ellipse, parabola and hyperbola studied as slices of a cone: the curves Kepler and Newton would need.

events.t: Hipparchus finds precession and begins trigonometry
events.n: Comparing his star positions with older ones reveals the slow drift of the equinoxes; his table of chords starts trigonometry.
Recovered from a shipwreck, this geared bronze calculator modelled the Sun and Moon, predicted eclipses and tracked the games.
The founding text of Chinese medicine: organs, channels, pulse diagnosis and the balance of yin and yang.
Stela 2 at Chiapa de Corzo carries the oldest known Long Count date; Maya place-value numbers came to include a zero.
Ten books on building, water supply, machines and sundials, the only major work on architecture surviving from antiquity.

events.t: Hero of Alexandria spins a sphere with steam
events.n: The aeolipile, turned by jets of steam, appears among Hero’s pneumatic devices, automata and surveying instruments.
A 37-book encyclopedia of astronomy, geography, animals, plants, medicine and minerals, read throughout the Middle Ages.
A court official presents paper made from bark, hemp, rags and old fishing nets: cheap writing material that spread across Asia.
Roman concrete with volcanic ash spans 43 metres, still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.
A bronze vessel that dropped a ball from a dragon’s mouth to signal a distant earthquake and the direction it came from.
An Earth-centred model of epicycles and equants that predicted planetary positions well enough to be used for 1,400 years.

events.t: Ptolemy maps the world by coordinates
events.n: Thousands of places listed by latitude and longitude, with instructions for projecting the globe onto a flat map.
Experiments on animals show that arteries carry blood and that cutting nerves from the spine paralyses muscles.
Problems solved with abbreviations for unknowns and powers, an early step towards algebraic notation.

events.t: Liu Hui’s commentary on the Nine Chapters
events.n: Proofs for the classic Chinese problem book, with negative numbers, elimination for linear systems and π ≈ 3.1416.
events.w: The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art

events.n: Head of a philosophical school, she wrote commentaries on Diophantus and Apollonius and helped edit Ptolemy’s Almagest.

events.t: Zu Chongzhi computes π to seven digits
events.n: π lies between 3.1415926 and 3.1415927, with the fraction 355/113: a record that stood for almost a thousand years.
Place-value arithmetic, a sine table, π ≈ 3.1416 and the proposal that the Earth turns on its axis.
Heavy and light bodies fall at nearly the same speed, and a thrown object keeps an impressed force, an early idea of impetus.
Two mathematicians design a vast dome carried on curved triangles over a square plan, a new solution in engineering.

events.t: Brahmagupta gives rules for zero and negatives
events.n: The first text to treat zero as a number, with rules for adding, subtracting and multiplying debts, fortunes and zero.

events.t: Sun Simiao’s prescriptions worth a thousand gold
events.n: A thirty-volume medical encyclopedia covering women’s and children’s health and diet, opening with a code of medical ethics.
The oldest complete star atlas known, drawing well over a thousand stars of the Chinese sky.
A water-powered globe with an escapement-like mechanism to mark the hours; Yi Xing also led a nationwide survey of the meridian.

events.t: Laboratory alchemy of the Jabirian corpus
events.n: Writings attributed to Jabir describe distillation, crystallisation and the preparation of acids, and sort substances by their properties.
Systematic solution of linear and quadratic equations; “algebra” comes from the book’s title and “algorithm” from his name.
Substitution ciphers are broken by counting how often each letter occurs: the start of cryptanalysis.

events.t: The Banu Musa’s Book of Ingenious Devices
events.n: About a hundred mechanisms, from automatic valves and self-trimming lamps to a programmable mechanical flute player.
A Taoist text warns that heating saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal together makes flames burst out: the first record of gunpowder.
Decades of observations at Raqqa give the length of the year to within about two minutes and improve on Ptolemy’s values.
His treatise on smallpox and measles gives the first clear clinical description separating the two diseases.
An illustrated star catalogue with the first written description of the Andromeda Galaxy, a “small cloud”.

events.t: Ibn Sahl states the law of refraction
events.n: A treatise on burning mirrors and lenses gives the sine law of refraction six centuries before Snell.
The last volume of his medical encyclopedia draws some 200 surgical instruments and was used in European schools for centuries.
Experiments with light, mirrors and the camera obscura show that we see by light entering the eye: a model of experimental method.

events.t: Al-Biruni measures the Earth from a hilltop
events.n: The dip of the horizon seen from a hill near Nandana gives the Earth’s radius to within a few per cent.
A five-book synthesis of Greek and Islamic medicine with rules for testing drugs, taught in Europe until the 1600s.
Characters of baked clay set in an iron frame, described by Shen Kuo, four centuries before Gutenberg.

events.t: Song astronomers record the Crab supernova
events.n: A “guest star” bright enough to see by day for 23 days; its remnant is the Crab Nebula.

events.t: Omar Khayyam: cubic equations and a new calendar
events.n: He classifies and solves cubic equations with conic sections, and leads the reform of the Jalali solar calendar at Isfahan.

events.t: Shen Kuo describes the magnetic compass
events.n: The Dream Pool Essays describe a magnetised-needle compass and magnetic declination, and argue that landscapes change over time.
A twelve-metre water-driven tower with an escapement that turned an armillary sphere and a celestial globe and struck the hours.
The head of the Ujjain observatory solves Pell’s equation by the cyclic method and touches on ideas of the derivative.
Books on plants, animals, stones and remedies, the first natural history and medicine written by a woman in Germany.

events.t: Al-Idrisi’s world map for Roger II
events.n: Fifteen years of travellers’ reports compiled at Palermo make the most accurate world map of the Middle Ages.
Hindu–Arabic numerals and place-value arithmetic for European merchants, with the rabbit problem behind the Fibonacci numbers.

events.t: Al-Jazari’s Book of Ingenious Mechanical Devices
events.n: Fifty machines, from crank-driven pumps to programmable automata, each drawn with instructions for building it.

events.t: Ibn al-Nafis describes the pulmonary circulation
events.n: Blood passes from the right side of the heart to the left through the lungs, not through pores in the wall as Galen taught.

events.t: The Maragheh observatory and the Tusi couple
events.n: Al-Tusi’s observatory produces new tables, and his two rolling circles turn circular motion into straight-line motion.

events.t: Roger Bacon’s Opus Majus urges experiment
events.n: A treatise for the Pope on optics, mathematics and “experimental science”, describing lenses that magnify.
Written during the siege of Lucera, the letter describes north and south poles, attraction and repulsion, and a pivoted compass.
New instruments and a network of observatories fix the year at 365.2425 days, the value of the later Gregorian calendar.
A Pisan sermon of 1306 says spectacles had been invented about twenty years before: convex lenses for reading.

events.t: Mondino de Luzzi’s manual of dissection
events.n: Written from public dissections at Bologna, his Anathomia was the standard anatomy text for two centuries.
Designed for St Albans Abbey, a mechanical clock showing the Sun, Moon, tides and eclipses, among the most complex of its age.

events.t: Oxford Calculators prove the mean speed theorem
events.n: A uniformly accelerating body covers the same distance as one moving at its mean speed, a result Galileo later used.
Models of the Moon and planets without Ptolemy’s equant, matching ones Copernicus used two centuries later.

events.t: Oresme draws graphs of changing quantities
events.n: Plotting intensity against time anticipates coordinate graphs and gives a geometric proof of the mean speed theorem.

events.t: Jikji printed with movable metal type
events.n: A Buddhist text printed at Heungdeok Temple, the oldest surviving book made with movable metal type.
The Kerala school expands π, sine and cosine as infinite series, some 250 years before Newton and Leibniz.

events.t: Al-Kashi computes π to 16 decimal places
events.n: A polygon with 805 million sides gives a record accuracy that stood for 180 years.
An automatic water clock for the Joseon court that announced the hours with bells, gongs and drums.
From a giant meridian arc at Samarkand, positions of nearly a thousand stars: the best catalogue between Ptolemy and Tycho.
Cast metal type, oil-based ink and a screw press make books cheap enough to spread learning across Europe.

events.t: Standard rain gauges across Joseon Korea
events.n: Identical gauges sent to every district produce the first systematic national records of rainfall.

events.t: Nilakantha Somayaji revises the planets’ orbits
events.n: A Kerala astronomer makes Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn circle the Sun, which in turn circles the Earth.
A world map showing a separate continent across the Atlantic, labelled “America” after Amerigo Vespucci.
Drawings made from dissection, of the heart’s valves, the spine and the foetus in the womb, far ahead of their time.
events.w: Science and inventions of Leonardo da Vinci

events.n: Lecturing at Basel he rejects the four humours for mineral remedies and careful dosing: the dose decides what is a poison.

events.t: Copernicus: the Earth orbits the Sun
events.n: A Sun-centred system explains the planets’ backward loops as an effect of the Earth’s own motion.

events.t: Vesalius’s Fabric of the Human Body
events.n: Seven illustrated books of anatomy from dissection, correcting hundreds of Galen’s errors.
events.w: De Humani Corporis Fabrica Libri Septem

events.t: Cardano solves cubic and quartic equations
events.n: General solutions of third- and fourth-degree equations, forcing mathematicians to handle square roots of negative numbers.
Diseases spread by tiny seeds, passed by touch, on objects or through the air: an early germ theory.
A vast illustrated encyclopedia of animals that marks the beginning of modern zoology.

events.t: Agricola’s On the Nature of Metals
events.n: The first systematic treatise on mining and metallurgy, with woodcuts of pumps, ventilation and smelting.
A world map on which a line of constant compass bearing is straight, the standard chart for navigation ever since.
A supernova shows no parallax, so it lies among the fixed stars: the heavens are not unchanging.
An island observatory whose instruments measure star positions to about an arcminute, the data Kepler later used.

events.t: Li Shizhen’s Compendium of Materia Medica
events.n: Twenty-seven years of work describe nearly 1,900 drugs from plants, animals and minerals, with over a thousand illustrations.
A short pamphlet makes decimal fractions practical for trade and measurement and calls for decimal units.
Spectacle makers in Middelburg put two lenses in a tube; who did it first is still disputed.

events.t: Gilbert: the Earth is a great magnet
events.n: Experiments with a magnetised sphere explain the compass needle and introduce the word “electric”.
Balls rolled down inclined planes show that the distance fallen grows with the square of the time.
Lipperhey asks the Dutch States-General for a patent on a tube for seeing distant things as if they were near.
From Tycho’s observations of Mars, the first two laws: elliptical orbits, and equal areas swept in equal times.
Mountains on the Moon, countless stars in the Milky Way and four moons circling Jupiter.
Tables that turn multiplication into addition, cutting the labour of astronomical calculation.
The square of a planet’s orbital period is proportional to the cube of its distance from the Sun.
Measurement shows the heart pumps far more blood than the body could make, so it must flow round a circuit.
events.w: Exercitatio Anatomica de Motu Cordis et Sanguinis in Animalibus

events.t: Descartes and Fermat unite algebra and geometry
events.n: Curves become equations in coordinates: analytic geometry, reached independently by Fermat.

events.t: Song Yingxing’s Works of Nature and Human Craft
events.n: An illustrated encyclopedia of Ming technology: farming, silk, salt, ceramics, metals, paper and weapons.
Written under house arrest at Arcetri: projectiles follow parabolas, and a mathematical science of the strength of materials.
A geared adding machine built to help his father with tax accounts, among the first mechanical calculators.
A tube of mercury upended in a bowl leaves a vacuum at the top, held up by the weight of the air.

events.t: Von Guericke’s air pump and evacuated hemispheres
events.n: Teams of horses cannot pull apart two copper hemispheres emptied of air, a public demonstration of air pressure.

events.t: Pascal and Fermat found probability theory
events.n: Letters on dividing the stakes of an unfinished game set out the mathematics of expected value.

events.t: Huygens finds Titan and Saturn’s ring
events.n: A better telescope reveals Saturn’s largest moon and explains the planet’s odd shape as a thin flat ring.
Clocks become accurate to seconds rather than minutes a day, making precise physics and astronomy possible.
Under the microscope a frog’s lung shows the tiny vessels linking arteries to veins, completing Harvey’s circuit.
Experiments with Hooke’s air pump show that a gas’s pressure varies inversely with its volume.
Engravings of a flea, a fly’s eye and cork, whose tiny compartments Hooke calls “cells”.
At home during the plague years Newton works out his method of fluxions, published only decades later.
A curved mirror in place of lenses removes the colour fringes that troubled refracting telescopes.
Boiling down urine in search of the philosopher’s stone yields a glowing substance, the first element found by a known person.
Layers of rock are laid down in order, the oldest at the bottom, and fossils are the remains of living things.

events.t: Cassini and Richer measure the Solar System
events.n: Simultaneous sightings of Mars from Paris and Cayenne give the first good estimate of the distance to the Sun.

events.t: Newton: white light is a mixture of colours
events.n: Prism experiments show sunlight splitting into a spectrum, with each colour bending by its own fixed amount.
Tiny single-lens microscopes reveal “little animals”, bacteria and protists, in rainwater and on teeth.

events.t: Rømer finds light has a finite speed
events.n: Eclipses of Jupiter’s moon Io come late when Jupiter is far from the Earth: light takes time to travel.
events.w: Rømer's determination of the speed of light

events.n: Every point on a wavefront sends out new wavelets, explaining reflection and refraction.
A Japanese mathematician uses determinants to eliminate unknowns from equations, ten years before Leibniz.
A paper in Acta Eruditorum introduces the d and ∫ notation still used today.

events.t: Newton’s Principia: motion and universal gravitation
events.n: Three laws of motion and an inverse-square law of gravity explain falling bodies, orbits, tides and Kepler’s laws.
Patented to drain mines, the first commercial use of steam to do work.
The comets of 1531, 1607 and 1682 are one body on a 76-year orbit; its return in 1758 confirms Newton’s gravity.

events.t: Merian paints the insects of Suriname
events.n: From two years’ fieldwork in Suriname, insects shown with their food plants through every stage of life.
Coke instead of charcoal frees iron-making from scarce wood, a foundation of the Industrial Revolution.
The first practical steam engine, pumping water from a coal mine near Dudley Castle.
Reliable mercury thermometers and, ten years later, the temperature scale that carries his name.

events.t: Onesimus’s inoculation saves lives in Boston
events.n: West African knowledge shared by Onesimus leads Boylston to inoculate during an epidemic, with far fewer deaths among those treated.

events.t: Montagu brings smallpox inoculation to Britain
events.n: Having seen the Ottoman practice in Constantinople, she has her daughter inoculated during a London epidemic.

events.t: Bradley discovers the aberration of starlight
events.n: Stars shift through the year because of the Earth’s motion: direct proof that the Earth orbits the Sun.

events.t: Gray shows electricity can be conducted
events.n: Charge travels hundreds of feet along a thread hung on silk, separating conductors from insulators.
The Earth’s rotation turns air flowing towards the equator into steady easterly winds.
A nested classification of nature into kingdoms, classes, orders, genera and species.

events.t: Euler and the bridges of Königsberg
events.n: Proving that no walk crosses each bridge exactly once, Euler founds graph theory.

events.t: The Earth is flattened at the poles
events.n: Measuring a degree of latitude in Lapland confirms Newton’s prediction of an Earth squashed at the poles.
events.w: French Geodesic Mission to the Equator

events.n: Faster-flowing fluid exerts less pressure; the book also explains gas pressure as molecules striking the walls.

events.t: Émilie du Châtelet’s Foundations of Physics
events.n: She argues that a body’s energy goes as the square of its speed and later translates Newton’s Principia with a commentary.
A hundred degrees between the freezing and boiling points of water, originally numbered the other way round.

events.t: The Leyden jar stores electric charge
events.n: A water-filled jar lined with metal holds a powerful charge: the first capacitor.
Twelve sick sailors get six different treatments; the two given oranges and lemons recover, an early controlled clinical trial.

events.t: Euler’s Introduction to the Analysis of the Infinite
events.n: Functions become the central objects of analysis, and exponentials are tied to sines and cosines.
A vast survey of nature that hints at species changing and at an Earth far older than scripture implied.
Experiments Franklin proposed, tried in France and with his kite, show lightning is an electrical discharge.

events.t: Linnaeus gives every plant a two-part name
events.n: Genus plus species for every known plant: the binomial names biology still uses.
“Fixed air” released from magnesia alba is a distinct gas, shown by careful weighing: quantitative chemistry begins.
His H4 watch keeps time across an Atlantic voyage to within seconds, solving the problem of longitude at sea.
Some 700 autopsies tie symptoms in life to damage in particular organs.

events.t: Lomonosov detects an atmosphere on Venus
events.n: As Venus crosses the Sun a bright rim appears around it: the planet has an atmosphere.
Published after his death by Price: how to update the probability of a hypothesis as evidence comes in.
“Inflammable air” from metals and acid is a distinct, very light gas; later he shows it burns to make water.
Condensing steam outside the cylinder cuts fuel use by about three-quarters, making steam power economical everywhere.
Air in which a candle has burned, stripped of fixed air, still will not support life or flame.
Priestley gets “dephlogisticated air” by heating mercury oxide; Scheele had already found it on his own.
The pull of a Scottish mountain on a plumb line gives the first estimate of the Earth’s mean density.
Burning is combination with oxygen, not the release of an imagined substance called phlogiston.

events.t: Ingenhousz: plants need light to refresh air
events.n: Only the green parts of plants, and only in sunlight, give off the air that keeps animals alive.
The first planet found with a telescope doubles the known size of the Solar System.
A star massive enough would hold back its own light: the first idea of a black hole.
The first crewed free flight drifts across Paris for about 25 minutes.
A torsion balance shows that electric force falls off with the square of the distance.
Slow erosion, deposition and uplift, repeated without end, imply an Earth vastly older than anyone thought.
A folk remedy tested on 163 patients becomes a standard treatment for dropsy.
The first of eight comets she found; she becomes the first woman in Britain paid for scientific work.
A list of elements, a new system of names and conservation of mass; Marie-Anne Lavoisier drew its plates.
Found in pitchblende and named after the recently discovered planet.
Frog legs twitch when touched with two different metals, linking nerves and electricity.
Stones and masses of iron fall from the sky, he argues, a view confirmed by the shower at L’Aigle in 1803.

events.t: Cuvier proves that species go extinct
events.n: Mammoth and mastodon bones differ from living elephants, so whole kinds of animal have died out.
The Solar System condensed from a rotating cloud of gas, refining an idea Kant had put forward in 1755.
Cowpox taken from a milkmaid protects a boy from smallpox: the first vaccine.
A torsion balance measures the tiny pull between lead spheres, giving the Earth’s density and, later, G.

events.t: The metre is defined from the Earth
events.n: A survey of the meridian from Dunkirk to Barcelona fixes the metre, made in platinum in 1799.
A thermometer beyond the red end of a prism’s spectrum warms most of all: invisible light.
A stack of zinc and copper discs separated by brine gives the first steady electric current.
Piazzi spots Ceres on New Year’s night; Gauss’s new orbit method lets astronomers find it again.
Modular arithmetic and quadratic reciprocity turn number theory into a systematic science.
Overlapping beams of light make bright and dark bands, strong evidence that light is a wave.
Silver chloride darkens fastest just beyond the violet end of the spectrum.
Each element is made of identical atoms with a characteristic weight, combining in simple ratios.

events.t: Hanaoka Seishū operates under general anaesthesia
events.n: A herbal anaesthetic lets him remove a breast tumour, forty years before ether was used in the West.
Chains of punched cards set the weaving pattern, an ancestor of programmable machines.
The first railway journey under steam hauls ten tons of iron and seventy men along a tramway.
A large battery splits molten potash and soda, revealing violently reactive new metals.
A cross-section of Chimborazo shows vegetation zones changing with altitude as with latitude: the start of biogeography.
Species change over time: the first full theory of evolution, though driven by inherited acquired traits.
Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure hold equal numbers of molecules.

events.t: Fraunhofer maps dark lines in sunlight
events.n: A precision spectroscope shows hundreds of dark lines in the Sun’s spectrum, later the key to what stars are made of.

events.t: William Smith’s geological map of Britain
events.n: The first geological map of a whole country, matching rock layers by the fossils they contain.

events.t: Sophie Germain’s theory of vibrating plates
events.n: Her prize-winning memoir on vibrating elastic surfaces lays groundwork for the theory of elasticity.
A rolled paper tube, then a wooden cylinder, lets doctors hear the heart and lungs clearly.
His theory predicts a bright spot in the shadow of a disc; Arago looks, and finds it.
A wire carrying current deflects a compass needle.
Limits and continuity defined precisely, ending a century of loose reasoning about infinitely small quantities.
A current-carrying wire circles continuously around a magnet: electricity turned into motion.
A design for a machine to compute and print mathematical tables automatically.
Any periodic signal can be written as a sum of sines and cosines, a tool now used across science.
The first complete skeleton of a long-necked sea reptile, one of the finds that revealed a lost world.
An engine’s best efficiency depends only on the temperatures it works between: the root of the second law.
events.w: Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire

events.n: The atmosphere lets sunlight in but slows the escape of heat, keeping the Earth warmer than it would otherwise be.
Bitumen hardened by light over a long exposure records the view from his window.
events.w: View from the Window at Le Gras

events.t: Brown sees particles jitter in water
events.n: Tiny particles from pollen dance endlessly, a motion Einstein would explain by molecules colliding.
The current through a conductor is proportional to the voltage across it.

events.t: Wöhler makes urea from inorganic matter
events.n: A substance known only from living things is made in the laboratory, undermining the idea of a vital force.
A consistent geometry in which Euclid’s parallel postulate fails, found by Lobachevsky and, in 1832, by Bolyai.
The Earth’s features are explained by processes still at work today, acting over immense spans of time.

events.t: Robert Brown names the cell nucleus
events.n: An opaque spot in orchid cells, which he then finds in plant cell after plant cell.
A changing magnetic field drives a current: the principle of every generator and transformer.
Set down the night before his fatal duel, his ideas on symmetry decide which equations can be solved by radicals.

events.t: Mary Somerville connects the physical sciences
events.n: A best-selling synthesis of the sciences; a review of it gives English the word “scientist”.
events.w: On the Connexion of the Physical Sciences

events.n: Motion in a rotating frame is deflected sideways, which shapes winds and ocean currents.

place.n: École Nationale des Ponts et Chaussées

events.n: Cooke and Wheatstone patent a needle telegraph; Morse’s code and single-wire system follow.

events.t: Bessel measures the distance to a star
events.n: The parallax of 61 Cygni puts it about ten light-years away, the first measured distance to a star.
All plants and animals are built of cells, the basic unit of life.
Silvered plates developed with mercury vapour make photography practical.
Plants draw nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium from the soil, the basis of chemical fertilisers.
Boulders and scratched rocks far from today’s glaciers show that ice once covered much of Europe.
Megalosaurus, Iguanodon and Hylaeosaurus are grouped as Dinosauria, “terrible lizards”.

place.n: Royal College of Surgeons of England

events.n: A wave’s frequency depends on how its source moves relative to the observer.

events.t: Ada Lovelace’s notes on the Analytical Engine
events.n: An algorithm for Bernoulli numbers, and the insight that such a machine could work on symbols, not just numbers.
Falling weights stirring water warm it by a fixed amount: heat is a form of energy.
He carves i² = j² = k² = ijk = −1 into a Dublin bridge: an algebra of rotations in three dimensions.
A public operation under ether in Boston launches surgical anaesthesia worldwide.
Le Verrier predicts a planet from Uranus’s wanderings; Galle finds it within a degree of the spot.
Energy changes form but its total stays the same, reached independently by Mayer, Joule and Helmholtz.

events.t: Semmelweis: wash hands to save mothers
events.n: Washing in chlorinated lime cuts deaths from childbed fever on his ward from about one in ten to one or two in a hundred.
The find wins a gold medal from the King of Denmark; she becomes America’s first professional woman astronomer.
A scale starting from absolute zero, the coldest temperature possible.
Heat never flows by itself from cold to hot; in 1865 Clausius names entropy.

events.t: Foucault’s pendulum shows the Earth turning
events.n: A 67-metre pendulum in the Panthéon slowly turns its plane of swing as the Earth rotates beneath it.
Logic becomes algebra on true and false, the basis of digital circuits.

events.t: John Snow traces cholera to a water pump
events.n: Mapping deaths around the Broad Street pump shows cholera spreads through water, a founding study of epidemiology.
A lecture extends geometry to any number of dimensions and any curvature: the mathematics of general relativity.
Blowing air through molten iron burns out the carbon, making steel cheaply and in bulk.

events.t: Eunice Foote: carbon dioxide traps heat
events.n: Glass cylinders of carbon dioxide warm far more in sunlight than air, and she suggests this could change the climate.

events.t: Perkin makes the first synthetic dye
events.n: An attempt to make quinine from coal tar yields a purple dye and launches the chemical industry.
Bones from a cave in the Neander valley are the first recognised fossils of an extinct kind of human.
Every cell comes from another cell, and disease is a disturbance of cells.
Her polar-area diagrams show most soldiers in the Crimea died of preventable disease, driving sanitary reform.
Wallace reaches natural selection on his own; his essay and Darwin’s notes are read together in London.
A white-light flare is followed by the strongest magnetic storm on record, with auroras worldwide and telegraphs failing.

events.t: Darwin’s On the Origin of Species
events.n: Evolution by natural selection explains the diversity and adaptations of life from common ancestors.

events.t: Kirchhoff and Bunsen invent spectral analysis
events.n: Each element emits and absorbs its own lines of colour, revealing what the Sun is made of.

events.t: Tyndall measures which gases absorb heat
events.n: Water vapour and carbon dioxide absorb infrared strongly, while oxygen and nitrogen hardly do.
A feathered fossil with teeth and a bony tail, found two years after Darwin predicted transitional forms.

events.t: Broca finds the brain’s speech area
events.n: A patient who could say only one word had damage to the left frontal lobe: functions are localised in the brain.

events.t: FitzRoy issues the first public weather forecasts
events.n: Observations gathered by telegraph give storm warnings and daily forecasts printed in The Times.
Boiled broth in swan-neck flasks stays sterile: microbes come only from microbes, a basis of germ theory.
Six carbon atoms in a ring explain benzene’s formula and the chemistry of aromatic compounds.
Electricity, magnetism and light are one phenomenon, waves in a field travelling at the speed of light.
Crossing thousands of pea plants shows traits passed on in discrete units, in predictable ratios.
The body keeps its internal environment constant, the idea later called homeostasis.
Carbolic acid on wounds and instruments sharply cuts deaths from infection after surgery.
Nitroglycerine soaked into diatomaceous earth becomes a safe, powerful explosive for mines and tunnels.
A yellow line seen during an eclipse in India fits no known element; Lockyer names it after the Sun.
A phosphorus-rich substance from the nuclei of white blood cells, “nuclein”, is the first isolation of DNA.
Elements in order of weight fall into families; gaps predict gallium, scandium and germanium.

place.n: St. Petersburg Practical Institute of Technology

events.n: Entropy is tied to the number of ways molecules can be arranged, explaining why time runs one way.
The real numbers cannot be listed one by one: some infinities are larger than others.
Four bonds pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron explain mirror-image molecules.

events.t: HMS Challenger sounds the deep ocean
events.n: A four-year voyage founds oceanography, finds thousands of new species and records depths in the Mariana Trench.

events.t: Koch proves a bacterium causes anthrax
events.n: Growing anthrax bacilli outside the body and following their life cycle ties one microbe to one disease.
Free energy and the phase rule explain when reactions run and how phases coexist.
Speech sent electrically along a wire.

events.t: Hall discovers the moons of Mars
events.n: Phobos and Deimos are found with the great refractor in Washington.
Sound recorded as grooves on tinfoil and played back.
Carbon filaments in a good vacuum glow for hundreds of hours, bringing electric light into homes.
A single-celled parasite in a patient’s blood: the first protozoan shown to cause disease.
Mobile cells in starfish larvae swarm round and engulf a thorn: the cellular immune response.
New staining methods reveal the cause of the deadliest disease of the age.
A car built around a petrol engine; Bertha Benz’s long drive in 1888 proves it practical.
A course of weakened virus saves a boy bitten by a rabid dog.
Light’s speed is the same in every direction: no sign of the ether thought to carry it.
Sparks across a gap send out invisible waves that reflect and refract like light, as Maxwell predicted.
A rotating magnetic field drives a motor without brushes, making AC power systems practical.

events.t: Cajal: the nervous system is made of separate cells
events.n: Golgi’s silver stain shows nerve cells are discrete units meeting at gaps, not one continuous net.
Serum from immunised animals neutralises bacterial toxins: the beginning of serum therapy.

events.t: Poincaré finds chaos in the three-body problem
events.n: Three gravitating bodies can move in ways so tangled that long-term prediction becomes impossible.
A skullcap and thighbone on Java are the first known fossils of Homo erectus.
Tobacco mosaic disease passes through filters that stop bacteria; in 1898 Beijerinck calls the agent a virus.
A dense leftover in air is a new inert element; neon, krypton and xenon follow, a whole new column of the table.

events.t: J. C. Bose demonstrates millimetre waves
events.n: Microwave apparatus and semiconductor detectors built in Calcutta send signals through walls to ring a bell.
Signals sent over a hill near Bologna; by 1901 they cross the Atlantic.
Rays from a discharge tube pass through flesh but not bone; within months doctors are using them.

events.t: Arrhenius calculates warming from carbon dioxide
events.n: Halving or doubling the carbon dioxide in the air would cool or warm the Earth by several degrees.
Uranium salts fog a wrapped photographic plate in the dark: atoms give off radiation by themselves.
Chickens fed polished rice fall ill and recover on unpolished rice, a path that led to the discovery of vitamins.
Juice pressed from yeast ferments sugar on its own: enzymes, not life itself, do the chemistry.

events.t: J. J. Thomson discovers the electron
events.n: Cathode rays are streams of particles far lighter than any atom, the first subatomic particle.
Malaria parasites in the gut of an Anopheles mosquito that had bitten an infected patient.

events.t: Marie and Pierre Curie discover polonium and radium
events.n: Tonnes of pitchblende processed by hand yield two new, intensely radioactive elements.
Acetylsalicylic acid, made at Bayer in 1897, goes on sale and becomes the world’s best-known drug.
Energy is given off in packets proportional to frequency, explaining the colour of hot bodies.
Red cells clump with some people’s serum but not others’: groups A, B and O make transfusion safe.
Stars sorted by their spectra into O, B, A, F, G, K, M; she classified some 350,000 by eye.
Secretin, carried in the blood, sets the pancreas working: chemical messengers, named hormones in 1905.
Dogs learn to salivate at a signal that predicts food: learned reflexes can be measured.

place.n: S. M. Kirov Military Medical Academy

events.n: A string galvanometer records the heart’s electrical activity precisely.
The first sustained, controlled, powered flight of a heavier-than-air machine.
The mathematics of reaching space with liquid-fuelled rockets in stages.
A two-electrode valve detects radio signals; with a third electrode, valves soon amplify them.
Light comes in quanta, each able to knock out one electron, the work cited in his Nobel Prize.

place.n: Swiss Federal Institute of Intellectual Property

events.t: Nettie Stevens finds the sex chromosomes
events.n: In mealworms the males carry a small Y chromosome: sex is set by chromosomes.
Space and time depend on motion, light’s speed is the same for all observers, and mass is energy: E = mc².

place.n: Swiss Federal Institute of Intellectual Property

events.n: Plant pigments separate into coloured bands as they wash through a column of chalk.
A shadow in earthquake waves on the far side of the Earth reveals a dense core at its centre.

events.t: Bakelite, the first fully synthetic plastic
events.n: Phenol and formaldehyde set into a hard, heat-proof material for the electrical age.
Exquisitely preserved soft-bodied animals from the Cambrian explosion of life.
He identifies the parasite, the insect that carries it and the disease itself in a single study.

events.t: Haber makes ammonia from the air
events.n: Nitrogen and hydrogen combine under pressure over a catalyst; scaled up by Bosch, it now feeds billions.

events.t: Mohorovičić finds the base of the crust
events.n: Earthquake waves speed up suddenly tens of kilometres down: the boundary between crust and mantle.
Compound 606, found by systematic screening, cures syphilis: a “magic bullet”.
A white-eyed fruit fly passes its trait on with the X chromosome; the Fly Room goes on to map genes.
Alpha particles bouncing back from gold foil show almost all of an atom’s mass sits in a tiny centre.
Plotting stars’ brightness against colour reveals the main sequence and the giants, the key to how stars evolve.
Mercury cooled with liquid helium to 4 kelvin loses all electrical resistance.
Matching coastlines, fossils and rocks suggest the continents were once joined and have moved apart.
Balloon flights to over 5 km show radiation increasing with height: it comes from space.
Spiral nebulae are rushing away at hundreds of kilometres a second, the first hint of cosmic expansion.
Brighter Cepheid variable stars pulse more slowly, a yardstick for cosmic distances.
Laue diffracts X-rays through crystals; the Braggs use it to read the positions of atoms.
X-ray spectra order the elements by nuclear charge, fixing the periodic table and its gaps.
Electrons keep to fixed orbits and give off light when they jump between them, explaining hydrogen’s spectrum.
A Madras clerk’s letter full of extraordinary formulas begins one of mathematics’ great collaborations.
An injectable form of chaulmoogra oil becomes the best leprosy treatment until the 1940s.
Gravity is the curving of spacetime by mass and energy.
Weeks after Einstein’s theory, an exact solution around a point mass, with a radius from which nothing escapes.

events.t: Shapley moves the Sun from the Galaxy’s centre
events.n: Globular clusters centre on a point far off in Sagittarius: the Milky Way is huge and we are off to one side.
Every symmetry of a physical system brings a conserved quantity, such as energy or momentum.

events.t: An eclipse confirms that gravity bends light
events.n: Stars near the eclipsed Sun appear shifted by the amount general relativity predicts.
Alpha particles knock hydrogen nuclei out of nitrogen: the first artificial nuclear reaction, and the proton.

events.t: The Bergen school describes weather fronts
events.n: Storms form along the boundaries between masses of warm and cold air.

events.t: Milanković links ice ages to the Earth’s orbit
events.n: Slow cycles in the shape of the Earth’s orbit and the tilt of its axis pace the ice ages.
Temperature decides how ionised a star’s gases are, which explains the sequence of stellar spectra.
A pancreatic extract keeps diabetic dogs alive; within months it saves a dying boy.
General relativity allows a universe that grows or shrinks rather than standing still.
X-rays bouncing off electrons lose energy like colliding balls: light carries momentum.

events.t: Hubble shows there are other galaxies
events.n: Cepheid stars in the Andromeda nebula put it far outside the Milky Way: a universe of galaxies.
Counting light quanta as identical reproduces Planck’s law; particles that obey it are called bosons.
Electrons, and all matter, behave as waves with a wavelength set by their momentum.
A child’s skull from South Africa with human-like teeth points to Africa as humanity’s birthplace.
No two electrons can share the same quantum state, which gives the periodic table its structure.
The first complete form of quantum mechanics, built only from quantities that can be observed.

events.t: Cecilia Payne: stars are mostly hydrogen
events.n: Applying Saha’s equation to stellar spectra shows stars are made mainly of hydrogen and helium.
A two-and-a-half-second flight from a farm opens the way to spaceflight.
An equation for the wave function predicts the energy levels of atoms.
Galaxy redshifts and relativity imply expansion; in 1931 he traces it back to a “primeval atom”.
Position and momentum cannot both be known exactly: a limit set by nature, not by instruments.
Joining quantum mechanics with relativity explains the electron’s spin and predicts the positron.
A mould contaminating a culture plate kills the bacteria around it.
Light scattered by molecules shifts in colour by amounts that identify the molecule.
Lactate from working muscle is turned back into glucose by the liver.

events.t: Hubble: galaxies recede in proportion to distance
events.n: The farther a galaxy, the faster it moves away: the universe is expanding.
A white dwarf heavier than about 1.4 Suns cannot support itself and must collapse further.
Blinking between photographic plates reveals a faint moving point beyond Neptune.
Particles spiral outwards in a magnetic field, gaining energy on every turn.
Magnetic lenses focus beams of electrons, eventually showing detail far below the limit of light.
Any consistent system strong enough for arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove.
A neutral particle in the nucleus explains atomic masses and becomes the key to fission.
A cloud-chamber track of a positive electron, the first antimatter, as Dirac predicted.

events.t: Jansky hears radio waves from the Milky Way
events.n: Static on a rotating antenna peaks towards the centre of the Galaxy: radio astronomy begins.

events.t: Cockcroft and Walton split the atom
events.n: Protons from an accelerator split lithium nuclei, and the energy released confirms E = mc².
Galaxies in the Coma Cluster move too fast to be held together by the matter we can see.
Probability rebuilt on measure theory, the foundation of modern statistics.

place.n: Schmidt Institute of Physics of the Earth

events.t: Irène and Frédéric Joliot-Curie make new radioactive atoms
events.n: Bombarding aluminium with alpha particles creates a radioactive form of phosphorus.

events.t: Yukawa’s theory of the nuclear force
events.n: A heavy particle passed between protons and neutrons explains the short reach of the strong force.
A synthetic polymer fibre made at DuPont, the first to succeed commercially.

events.t: Domagk’s Prontosil, the first sulfa drug
events.n: A red dye cures streptococcal infections in mice and then people, the first widely effective antibacterial.
Radio echoes from a bomber flying near Daventry show aircraft can be detected far away.
A logarithmic scale compares the sizes of earthquakes from seismograph readings.

events.t: Inge Lehmann discovers the inner core
events.n: Faint earthquake waves inside the core’s shadow reveal a solid inner core.
A simple imagined machine defines computation and shows some problems can never be solved by algorithm.
Whittle runs the first turbojet on a test bed; von Ohain’s engine powers the first jet flight in 1939.
A loop of reactions in the cell burns fuel molecules to release energy.
Liquid helium below 2.2 kelvin flows without any viscosity.

place.n: P.L. Kapitza Institute for Physical Problems RAS

events.n: A fish known only from fossils 66 million years old turns up in a trawler’s catch off South Africa.
Uranium hit by neutrons yields barium; Meitner and Frisch explain it as the nucleus splitting in two.

events.t: Pauling’s Nature of the Chemical Bond
events.n: Quantum mechanics explains how atoms bond, with electronegativity and hybrid orbitals.
The last element to be discovered in nature, found in the decay of actinium.
Hydrogen fuses into helium through the proton–proton chain and the carbon cycle, powering the Sun.
Purified penicillin protects infected mice; mass production follows in time for D-Day.

place.n: Sir William Dunn School of Pathology

events.t: Plutonium and the first elements beyond uranium
events.n: Neptunium and plutonium, heavier than uranium, are made with the cyclotron.
An electromechanical machine that runs programs from punched film, in binary floating point.
A pile of graphite and uranium under a Chicago stadium sustains a controlled chain reaction.
A patent for jam-proof radio guidance that hops between frequencies, a forerunner of modern wireless.
Valve machines help break the German high command’s cipher.
A rotating-drum dialyser, built under occupation, keeps patients with failing kidneys alive.

events.t: Streptomycin, the first drug against tuberculosis
events.n: Isolated from soil bacteria by the student Albert Schatz in Waksman’s laboratory.
Purified DNA turns harmless bacteria into virulent ones: genes are made of DNA.
The Manhattan Project’s test in New Mexico releases energy equal to about twenty thousand tonnes of TNT.
A general-purpose electronic computer of some 18,000 valves, programmed by a team of six women.
Random sampling on early computers solves problems too complex for exact methods.
A germanium device amplifies signals, replacing valves and making modern electronics possible.
A hot early universe would forge hydrogen and helium in the observed amounts and leave a faint afterglow.
Information measured in bits, and the limits to sending it reliably over a noisy channel.
The Manchester Baby runs a program held in its own electronic memory.
Renormalisation tames the infinities, making QED the most precisely tested theory in physics.
The steady decay of carbon-14 dates once-living material up to about 50,000 years old.
Protons and neutrons fill shells, explaining the “magic numbers” of especially stable nuclei.
In maize, some pieces of DNA move around the genome and switch other genes on and off.
ENIAC computes a 24-hour forecast, the start of numerical weather prediction.

events.t: HeLa, the first immortal human cell line
events.n: Cells taken without consent from Henrietta Lacks’s tumour grow indefinitely and power decades of research.
The 21-centimetre line lets radio astronomers map the spiral arms of the Milky Way.
A program that translates symbolic code into machine instructions, leading to languages such as COBOL.
Radioactive labels show that viruses inject their DNA, not their protein, into bacteria.
Sparks through simple gases produce amino acids: the building blocks of life from chemistry alone.
A substance from mouse tumours makes nerve fibres sprout, the first growth factor known.
An X-ray diffraction image of DNA whose cross-shaped pattern reveals a helix.
Two complementary strands wound in a helix suggest at once how genetic information is copied.
events.w: Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids: A Structure for Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid

events.t: Marie Tharp finds the Mid-Atlantic rift
events.n: Plotting sonar soundings reveals a valley along the crest of the ridge, evidence that the seafloor spreads.
Sunlight turned into electricity at about 6% efficiency, the first practical solar cell.
Time kept by the vibrations of caesium atoms; in 1967 the second itself is redefined by them.
The first full amino-acid sequence of a protein: every protein has a precise chemical structure.
A trial involving well over a million children shows the inactivated vaccine works.
Lead isotopes in meteorites give 4.55 billion years; Patterson goes on to expose lead pollution.
Antineutrinos from a nuclear reactor are caught in tanks of water, 26 years after Pauli proposed them.
X-ray crystallography and early computers reveal the structure of a large, vital molecule.
Nuclear reactions in stars and supernovae build every element heavier than helium.
Electrons pair up through vibrations of the crystal and move without resistance.

events.t: Wu shows nature tells left from right
events.n: Electrons from decaying cobalt-60 prefer one direction, overturning the conservation of parity.
A small beeping sphere in orbit opens the space age.
Kilby’s germanium chip, then Noyce’s planar silicon one, put whole circuits on a single piece of semiconductor.
Continuous measurements show the carbon dioxide in the air rising year after year.
Explorer 1’s Geiger counter finds zones of trapped charged particles around the Earth.
A robust 1.8-million-year-old skull at Olduvai Gorge pushes human origins deep into Africa’s past.
Radioactive tracers measure tiny amounts of hormones in blood, transforming endocrinology.

events.t: Jane Goodall sees chimpanzees make tools
events.n: A chimpanzee strips a twig to fish for termites: making tools is not uniquely human.
A ruby crystal produces the first coherent beam of light.
Synthetic RNA made only of uracil yields a chain of phenylalanine; by 1966 all 64 codons are read.

place.n: United States National Institutes of Health

events.t: How genes are switched on and off
events.n: A regulatory switch in bacteria shows how cells control which genes are active.

events.t: Gagarin, the first human in space
events.n: One orbit of the Earth in 108 minutes.
A glowing jellyfish protein, isolated by Shimomura, later becomes a universal tag for watching genes at work.
The harm pesticides such as DDT do to wildlife launches the modern environmental movement.
A simple weather model is so sensitive to its starting point that long-range forecasting is impossible.
The spectrum of 3C 273 is hugely redshifted: a starlike point billions of light-years away, outshining galaxies.
Stripes on the ocean floor record new crust forming at ridges while the Earth’s magnetic field flips.
A faint microwave hiss from every direction is the afterglow of the Big Bang.
A field filling space gives particles their mass and implies a new particle.
Protons, neutrons and their relatives are built from three kinds of smaller particle.
An algorithm that makes digital signal processing fast enough to be everywhere.
A liquid-crystal polymer solution spun into fibres five times stronger than steel for their weight.
Kao shows that purified glass fibres could carry light signals over long distances.
The first realistic computer model of the atmosphere predicts about 2 °C of warming if carbon dioxide doubles.
Electromagnetism and the weak force are two faces of one interaction, a pillar of the Standard Model.

events.t: Lynn Margulis: cells merged to build complex life
events.n: Mitochondria and chloroplasts began as free-living bacteria taken inside other cells.
In Cape Town, Louis Washkansky receives a donor heart and lives for 18 days.
The Earth’s surface is a mosaic of rigid plates whose motions explain earthquakes, volcanoes and mountains.
A radio source ticking every 1.34 seconds turns out to be a spinning neutron star.

events.t: Kimura’s neutral theory of molecular evolution
events.n: Most changes in DNA are neither helpful nor harmful and spread by chance.
A drink of water, salt and sugar saves cholera patients; it goes on to save millions of children.
Humans walk on another world; the guidance software led by Margaret Hamilton copes with alarms during the landing.
A computer at UCLA sends “lo” to Stanford before crashing: the internet’s ancestor.
An image sensor that turned photography and astronomy digital.
Some viruses copy RNA back into DNA, breaking the one-way flow of genetic information.
Stars at the edge of Andromeda orbit as fast as those near the centre: evidence for dark matter.
X-ray slices put together by computer give the first cross-sectional image of a living brain.
A star orbiting an unseen companion too heavy to be a neutron star.
A whole computer processor on one chip of 2,300 transistors.
Some problems are as hard as every problem whose answers are easy to check: the P versus NP question.
A fourth-century herbal text leads her to a cold extract of sweet wormwood that cures malaria.
Hybrid rice raises yields by about a fifth, helping to feed hundreds of millions.
Magnetic field gradients turn nuclear magnetic resonance into images of the body.
Genes cut and pasted into bacterial plasmids are copied by the bacteria: genetic engineering begins.

events.t: Asymptotic freedom completes the Standard Model
events.n: Quarks bind ever more weakly at short range, making the theory of the strong force work.
Chlorine from refrigerant gases destroys ozone high in the atmosphere in a chain reaction.
Quantum effects make black holes glow faintly and slowly evaporate.
A 3.2-million-year-old skeleton shows our ancestors walked upright long before their brains grew large.

events.t: TCP/IP joins networks into an internet
events.n: A protocol for linking separate networks into one, adopted across ARPANET in 1983.
Self-similar shapes describe coastlines, clouds and markets; he coins the word “fractal”.
Immune cells fused with cancer cells make unlimited amounts of a single antibody.

events.t: The four colour theorem proved by computer
events.n: The first major theorem proved with essential help from a computer.
Two parties agree a secret over an open line; RSA follows a year later.
A compound from a mould blocks the body’s cholesterol production; statins become among the most used drugs.

place.n: Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology

events.n: Ribosomal RNA reveals a third domain of life alongside bacteria and eukaryotes.
The submersible Alvin finds rich communities living on chemical energy from the vents, not sunlight.
Chain-terminating nucleotides read DNA letter by letter; the first DNA genome follows.
Twin spacecraft tour Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune; Voyager 1 reaches interstellar space in 2012.

events.t: The first baby conceived by IVF
events.n: Louise Brown is born after fertilisation outside the body.
A soil microbe from Japan yields a drug against river blindness and elephantiasis.

events.t: An asteroid ended the age of dinosaurs
events.n: A layer of clay rich in iridium, first studied at Gubbio, marks a giant impact 66 million years ago.

events.t: Genes that lay out the embryo
events.n: A search through fruit-fly mutants finds the genes that set up the body plan.
A burst of runaway expansion in the first instant explains why the universe is so uniform and flat.
Electrical resistance comes in exact steps set only by fundamental constants.
The first human disease wiped out, after a worldwide campaign of vaccination and surveillance.
A tip a few atoms wide images individual atoms on a surface.
Entangled photons break Bell’s limit: quantum correlations cannot be explained by hidden local causes.
Helicobacter pylori, not stress, causes most ulcers; Marshall drinks a culture to prove it.
Misfolded proteins, with no genetic material, cause infectious brain diseases.
An alloy with five-fold symmetry, ordered but never repeating, a pattern thought impossible.

place.n: National Institute of Standards and Technology

events.n: A new retrovirus isolated from a patient’s lymph node turns out to cause AIDS.
Cycles of heating and copying multiply a stretch of DNA a billion times over.
The carriers of the weak force are found at the masses the theory predicted.
Repeated stretches of DNA give a pattern unique to each person.
An enzyme that rebuilds the ends of chromosomes, linking cell ageing and cancer.
Stretching, amplifying and squeezing laser pulses gives ultra-short, ultra-intense light, now used in eye surgery.
Sixty carbon atoms form a hollow ball: a new form of carbon.
Building on Whittingham’s and Goodenough’s electrodes, Yoshino makes a safe, rechargeable cell.
Spring ozone over Antarctica has fallen by a third; the Montreal Protocol follows in 1987.
A copper-oxide ceramic superconducts at 35 kelvin, far above any metal; others soon pass liquid-nitrogen temperature.
The nearest supernova in centuries; neutrinos from the collapsing core are detected on Earth.
Bubbles of ancient air show carbon dioxide and temperature rising and falling together for 160,000 years.
A proposal for linked hypertext over the internet, with the first browser and server running by 1990.
Above the atmosphere, once its mirror is corrected, it measures the age and expansion of the universe.
A buried crater some 180 km wide in Yucatán is the impact behind the extinction of the dinosaurs.

events.t: Ripples in the cosmic microwave background
events.n: COBE measures the background’s perfect heat spectrum and the tiny ripples that seeded galaxies.
The first object found beyond Neptune after Pluto reveals a belt of icy bodies.

events.t: The first planets beyond the Solar System
events.n: Timing a pulsar reveals planets of a few Earth masses orbiting it.
Gallium nitride LEDs complete the set of colours, making white LED lighting possible.
A 350-year-old problem falls through the modularity of elliptic curves.
events.w: Wiles's proof of Fermat's Last Theorem

events.n: A quantum computer could factor large numbers exponentially faster, threatening today’s encryption.

events.t: A planet around a Sun-like star
events.n: A giant planet on a four-day orbit, found by the wobble it gives its star.
Rubidium atoms cooled to billionths of a degree merge into a single quantum state.
The first mammal cloned from an adult cell.
Sinosauropteryx from north-east China shows simple feathers on a dinosaur, tying dinosaurs to birds.

events.t: The universe’s expansion is speeding up
events.n: Distant supernovae are fainter than expected, pointing to a mysterious dark energy.
Cells able to become any tissue are grown in the laboratory.
Neutrinos change type as they travel, which requires them to have mass.
Double-stranded RNA silences matching genes, a new layer of gene control.
Atomic maps of the cell’s protein factory, after decades of work.
The Hubble Space Telescope Key Project measures the universe’s expansion rate to about ten per cent.

events.t: A giant black hole at the Milky Way’s centre
events.n: Stars orbiting an unseen object of four million solar masses show it must be a black hole.
An international consortium reads the three billion letters of human DNA.

place.n: United States National Institutes of Health

events.n: Ricci flow settles a century-old question about three-dimensional shapes; he declines the Fields Medal.
Sticky tape peels carbon into sheets one atom thick, astonishingly strong and conductive.

events.t: Tiktaalik, a fish on its way to land
events.n: A 375-million-year-old fish with a neck and limb-like fins, found where theory said to look.

events.t: Grid cells, the brain’s coordinate system
events.n: Neurons fire on a hexagonal grid as an animal moves, letting the brain map space.

place.n: Norwegian University of Science and Technology

events.n: Four genes turn adult skin cells back into stem cells.

events.t: Water found across the Moon’s surface
events.n: Instruments on India’s Chandrayaan-1 detect water and hydroxyl across the lunar surface.
Ancient DNA shows people outside Africa carry some Neanderthal genes; the Denisovans are identified the same year.

place.n: Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology

events.n: A bacterial enzyme guided by RNA cuts DNA at any chosen spot.

events.t: Deep learning wins at image recognition
events.n: A deep neural network trained on graphics chips wins the ImageNet challenge by a wide margin.
The ATLAS and CMS experiments at the Large Hadron Collider find the particle predicted in 1964.
Infinitely many pairs of primes lie less than 70 million apart, a first step towards the twin prime conjecture.
Work on the dynamics and geometry of Riemann surfaces makes her the first woman to win the Fields Medal.
Ripples in spacetime from two merging black holes, a century after Einstein predicted them.
Fossils of a new human species from a deep chamber of a South African cave.

events.t: An orbital rocket booster lands upright
events.n: A first stage returns to land after a launch to orbit, making rockets reusable.

events.t: Viazovska solves sphere packing in eight dimensions
events.n: Using modular forms she proves the E8 lattice is the densest packing in eight dimensions.
A design built on attention that underlies today’s large language models.

events.t: The first image of a black hole
events.n: A planet-wide array of radio dishes images the shadow of the black hole in the galaxy M87.
An AI system predicts the 3D shapes of proteins from their sequences with near-experimental accuracy.
Modified messenger RNA, made safe by Karikó and Weissman, gives COVID-19 vaccines within a year.
A deliberate collision shortens the orbit of Dimorphos, the first test of planetary defence.
Laser-driven fusion releases more energy than the lasers deliver to the fuel.

events.t: The James Webb Space Telescope’s first images
events.n: An infrared observatory 1.5 million km away sees galaxies from the universe’s first few hundred million years.

events.t: A landing near the Moon’s south pole
events.n: India’s Chandrayaan-3 makes the first soft landing in the Moon’s south polar region.

events.t: Samples from the far side of the Moon
events.n: China’s Chang’e 6 brings back the first rock and soil from the lunar far side.

events.t: The complete wiring of a fly’s brain
events.n: The FlyWire project maps all 140,000 neurons and some 50 million connections of an adult fruit fly.
A team of nine mathematicians completes a proof of some 800 pages connecting geometry and number theory.

events.t: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s first light
events.n: The largest digital camera ever built begins a ten-year survey of the southern sky.

Q1035.name: Charles Darwin
country: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

Q1043.name: Carl Linnaeus
Q1043.desc: Swedish botanist, physician, and zoologist (1707–1778); developed the foundations of modern taxonomy

Q1290.name: Blaise Pascal
